comments.body: Tag prefix plus a lifecycle rule. Branch builds get tags like branch-sha and expire after 14 days, anything that reaches production is retagged release-version and never touched by the rule. No extra registry to run, and retagging does not copy layers, so it costs nothing.

title: Lighthouse score in CI varies by 6 points between runs, what do you gate on
body: Our Vue checkout has a CI step that fails the build when the Lighthouse performance score drops under 85. It fails at random, because the same commit scores anywhere between 82 and 89. Do you gate on the score at all? I am thinking of switching to a budget on JavaScript bytes, request count and layout shift, and keeping Lighthouse as a report people read, not a gate.

comments.body: Run it five times and take the median. Gate on the median.
Five runs of Lighthouse is four extra minutes on every pull request. I would run three on pull requests and a bigger batch nightly, and compare the nightly trend, not a single run.
Nightly misses regressions at the time they are introduced, which is when they are cheapest to fix. By the time you see the trend, five merges have happened. I would rather pay the minutes on the PR.

Also check where it runs. A shared runner with noisy neighbours gives you a different CPU every time and the score follows it. A small dedicated runner for these checks removed half of the variance for us.
I gate on JavaScript bytes only, because it is deterministic. We set a limit 5 percent above the current size and fail the PR when it passes. Dull, and it works.

Maybe look at real user data instead, if the shop has enough visitors. Lab scores say little about what a shopper on an older phone actually sees. Field metrics from real sessions are noisier but they are the truth.
It depends on traffic. If the shop has a few hundred visits a day, field data takes weeks to be meaningful, so lab numbers are all you have for decisions. How many visits do you have?

Deterministic checks for the gate: bytes, request count, number of third party scripts. Lighthouse in a comment on the PR for humans. Mixing the two is the problem, because a flaky gate teaches the team to ignore red.
Bytes and request count do not catch layout shift, which is what usually breaks checkout (a banner pushes the pay button down just as someone taps). That one needs a real browser check.

Not my field, but in firmware we have the same issue with timing measurements. We gate on counts and only record timing. A layout shift number from the lab is noisy for the same reason, so maybe use a fixed viewport and no network variance.
Pin the Chrome version and the Lighthouse version. A silent upgrade of the runner image shifted our scores by 4 points overnight and we blamed the code for two days.

This is the direction I am going: budgets on bytes, request count and third party scripts as the gate, plus a layout shift check in a real browser with three runs. Lighthouse report posted as a PR comment, never red.

Check the time to first byte on the staging server before blaming the front end. If the backend has a cold database cache on the first request of a run, you get a swing that has nothing to do with the Vue code.
We went through this and ended up gating on nothing and watching a weekly report. A gate that people can bypass with a rerun is worse than no gate. Honest result, I know it will not please everyone.

body: Spring : un traitement d'import de commandes ne fait pas de rollback quand une ligne échoue. La méthode transactionnelle est appelée depuis une autre méthode de la même classe, donc l'annotation est ignorée (auto-invocation). Je vois deux sorties : extraire la méthode dans un autre bean, ou utiliser un TransactionTemplate dans le code. Laquelle gardez-vous dans une base de code que d'autres vont lire ?

comments.body: Extraire dans un autre bean. C'est plus de classes mais le comportement est visible dans la structure. Un TransactionTemplate dans le code marche aussi, mais on oublie vite pourquoi il est là. Garde un commentaire qui explique l'auto-invocation, ça vaut plus que le choix.

Je viens de Python donc ça m'est étranger, mais je trouve effrayant qu'une annotation soit ignorée sans avertissement. Chez nous la transaction est un bloc with bien visible. Le TransactionTemplate me semble plus honnête, on voit où ça commence et où ça finit.

Pense aussi à ce qui doit être annulé : si l'import appelle un service externe pour chaque ligne, le rollback de la base n'annule pas ces appels. Une transaction par ligne avec un rapport d'erreurs est peut-être plus adaptée qu'un tout ou rien.

body: Rust worker that claims jobs from a Postgres table with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a sqlx transaction. When a job panics, I see the row stay locked for about 30 seconds before another worker can take it. My understanding is that the transaction rolls back on drop, but the rollback is queued, not instant. Is that what I am seeing, or is the connection returned to the pool still inside the transaction? How do you guarantee release on panic?

Each pull request gets its own namespace with the app and its own Postgres seeded from a nightly 6 GB snapshot. Ready time is about 7 minutes, almost all of it the restore, and reviewers stop waiting. Options: a shared database with one schema per preview, volume snapshots that clone copy-on-write so the database starts in seconds, or a trimmed anonymised dataset of about 400 MB that restores in 40 seconds but may hide the bugs that need volume. Cloning depends on the storage class we can get. I lean toward the small dataset, with the full one on a nightly job.

comments.body: For design review we mostly need the screens, so the small dataset works if it includes the awkward data: very long names, empty states, users with 500 items and users with none. Those are the cases that break layouts. A 400 MB dataset picked at random will lack them.

body: Un index partiel sur les ordonnances non délivrées (WHERE delivree = false) a ramené la liste du jour de 900 ms à 15 ms. La table fait 2 millions de lignes et 98 % sont déjà délivrées, donc l'index est minuscule. On m'a laissé toucher à la base de dev, et c'est le backend qui l'a repris en migration.

comments.body: Attention, le planificateur n'utilise l'index que si la requête contient une condition qui implique celle de l'index. Si l'ORM écrit « delivree IS NOT TRUE » ou passe le booléen en paramètre lié, il peut l'ignorer selon les cas. Vérifie avec EXPLAIN en prod.
Et si la proportion change un jour, que le stock non délivré grossit, l'index grossit aussi. Ce n'est pas un problème tant que les non délivrées restent peu nombreuses, mais à surveiller.
Bonne remarque pour le paramètre lié. Je vérifie : en dev l'ORM écrit bien delivree = false en littéral, donc il est utilisé. Mais je vais demander une vérification en prod avant de me réjouir.
Un index partiel est un des outils les plus sous-utilisés de Postgres. On en a un sur les commandes en cours, quelques centaines de Ko pour des millions de lignes.
Je me demande comment vous faites quand la requête filtre aussi par pharmacie. Index partiel plus la colonne pharmacie dans l'index ? J'ai du mal à voir quand ça vaut la peine d'ajouter la colonne.
Je note, je ne savais pas que ça existait. Je pensais que les index étaient toujours sur toute la table.
Ça existe depuis longtemps. À essayer sur les colonnes où une valeur est rare et souvent demandée, comme un statut « en attente ».

title: Ship the tokenizer and the training image as one versioned bundle
body: Last month we upgraded the tokenizer library for a local-language model. The same Arabic and Darija strings with diacritics got split differently, and the evaluation numbers moved by 2 points for reasons nobody could find for a week. Proposal: the training Docker image bakes in the tokenizer files and records their hash, the model artifact stores that hash and the image tag, and loading a model with a mismatched tokenizer fails with a clear message. Costs: every tokenizer change means a new image and a retrain decision. Undecided: whether the hash covers the normalisation rules or only the vocabulary.

comments.body: What would a user of the model notice without this? I would have guessed a 2 point change is invisible, and I do not know whether to care when I see it on a dashboard.
Hash the normalisation rules too, otherwise the check passes with the same vocabulary and different splits, which is exactly your case. I would hash the whole tokenizer folder, not pick files.

body: Quatrième édition du tableau de bord du festival : 3 200 visiteurs en même temps sur la page programme, aucun souci. Ce qui a tout changé, c'est un cache HTTP de 30 secondes avec stale-while-revalidate devant l'API. Le serveur a vu environ une requête sur quarante.

comments.body: Une requête sur quarante, c'est bien. Mais attention à stale-while-revalidate sur des données que les gens regardent pour décider : si le programme change à la dernière minute, un visiteur voit encore l'ancienne séance pendant la fenêtre de revalidation. Tu as des données qui ne doivent jamais être périmées ?
Pour un programme de festival, 30 secondes de retard ne gênent personne. Ça devient gênant pour des disponibilités de billets. Je mettrais une durée différente par route, pas un réglage global.
Ça passe par Nginx ou par un CDN ? Si c'est Nginx sur un seul serveur, quand il tombe tu perds tout le bénéfice. Chez nous un CDN devant absorbait aussi les pics de lecture.
Un CDN devant, avec le serveur d'origine sur un petit VPS. C'est le CDN qui fait le stale-while-revalidate, l'origine renvoie juste les en-têtes Cache-Control.
Les billets, non, ils ne passent pas par ce cache : la route de réservation a un Cache-Control no-store. Je n'ai mis le cache que sur le programme et la liste des films.
Un CDN, oui, mais fais attention aux requêtes avec cookie : si le CDN voit un cookie de session, il peut ne rien mettre en cache. J'ai passé une journée là-dessus.
Oui, on a eu ça aussi. La solution était de ne pas envoyer de cookie sur les routes publiques, ou de configurer le CDN pour ignorer le cookie sur ces chemins.
J'ajouterais qu'il faut regarder le taux de hits du CDN une fois par semaine. Une configuration qui marchait peut se casser sans bruit quand quelqu'un ajoute un en-tête Vary.
Garde ce ratio comme indicateur et mets une alerte : si on passe d'une requête sur quarante à une sur dix, quelque chose a cassé le cache.

body: A Vue 3 watcher with deep true on the cart object ran 40 times when one quantity changed, because we were replacing the nested items array on every update. Watching just the computed total and the item count made the extra renders go away.

comments.body: Not frontend, but I see the same shape on the backend: a trigger that fires for every row of a bulk update because someone wrote it for single updates. Is replacing the whole array needed, or could you update in place?

Does the replace happen because the API returns the whole cart after each change? If so I would make the response diff-friendly rather than fixing it with watchers on the client. Which of the two do you control?

Both, though the API is shared with the mobile app, so changing the response means a version bump. For now the watcher fix is cheap. I may add a version of the endpoint that returns only changed lines and let the app move over slowly.

title: Camera and notification permissions for first-time smartphone users, when to ask
body: Designing onboarding for a Flutter app for first-time smartphone users. We need camera and notification permissions. Do we ask both on first launch before anything else, or ask each when the feature is first used? Store reviews already say the app is "asking too much" and I do not know which choice they mean.

comments.body: When the feature is used, always. A permission dialog with no context gets denied, and on Android after two denials you may not be able to ask again without sending people to settings. Show one sentence of why before the system dialog.

For the camera, yes. For notifications I would ask after the first completed action, not at the moment of use, because at the moment of use people are busy. Then you have a reason to show and a person who has already seen the value.

The moment after the first completed action is good. Be careful with the screen: a soft screen of our own first, with Yes and Not now, protects the one-shot system dialog. If they say Not now we can ask again in a week, the system one only once on iOS.

How many of those store reviews are about permissions and how many about something else? A line that says "asking too much" may be about login or a phone number field. Reading ten of them might point somewhere else.
Good point. I would also read them in the original language. A comment in French or Arabic that was translated automatically sometimes says something different from what the person wrote.
